title: WhatFlow Chat Automation vs Business API: pricing, ratings and reliability
excerpt: Two WhatFlow apps, two connection methods and separate ratings. Safwan Adnan explains linked-device automation, official Meta Cloud API, pricing and who should use each.
verdict: WhatFlow has two separate Shopify apps. Chat Automation is our lower-barrier linked-device option, currently recommended only for small and startup stores with modest workloads. WhatFlow WhatsApp Business API uses the official Meta Cloud API and is our recommendation for growing stores and important automated messaging. The older app’s 3.9 rating and Business API’s 5.0 rating belong to separate listings, checked October 24, 2026.

children.text: The short answer: WhatFlow has two different Shopify apps

WhatFlow Chat Automation and WhatFlow WhatsApp Business API are separate apps from the same developer, Scrptble. The older listing is publicly named “WhatFlow: Whatsapp Automation.” It connects through the linked-device method. The newer listing, “WhatFlow WhatsApp Business API,” connects through the official Meta Cloud API. They share a brand and an ecommerce focus, but they should not be treated as the same product with one combined rating.

I’m Safwan Adnan, co-founder and CEO of WhatFlow. If you are deciding between them today, my recommendation is straightforward: consider Chat Automation only for a small or startup store with modest messaging needs and tolerance for connection interruptions. Choose Business API when customer communication is important to daily operations, when the store is growing, or when you want the official platform foundation for automation.
In this page’s comparison table, the WhatFlow column means WhatFlow WhatsApp Business API. The other column means the older Chat Automation app.
Why does WhatFlow have a 3.9-star rating?

The 3.9-star rating belongs to WhatFlow: Whatsapp Automation, our older linked-device app at apps.shopify.com/whatflow. As of October 24, 2026, that listing shows 336 reviews. It launched on October 21, 2024, so it has more than two years of merchant history.

WhatFlow WhatsApp Business API has its own listing at apps.shopify.com/whatflow-official-api. It launched on May 8, 2026 and shows a 5.0-star rating from 51 reviews on the same checked date. A search result that attaches the older app’s 3.9 rating to the newer Business API product is mixing two separate listings.

The older reviews are real feedback and deserve to be read. The explanation is not that a lower rating should be ignored; it is that the buyer needs the right product name, connection method, review dates and intended workload. A newer perfect score also comes from a smaller review history. Ratings change, so the two linked Shopify listings remain the place to check the current figures.
What changed for the older linked-device product?

Our original app made Shopify WhatsApp automation accessible to merchants who wanted a low barrier to entry. A small store could connect its number through a linked device and begin with practical work such as order confirmations or fulfillment updates. For a founder handling early orders personally, that simplicity and low messaging cost could be a useful starting point.

From our team’s experience supporting merchants, the linked-device experience also became harder to rely on as WhatsApp enforcement and connection behavior changed. We saw interruptions and number restrictions affecting some stores, particularly when workloads became larger. This is our account of support experience, not an independent finding that one policy change caused every negative review. The public listing also contains connection complaints and our responses, so merchants can inspect that history themselves.

Some stores previously ran larger workloads successfully. That history does not change our current recommendation: we now position Chat Automation for small and startup stores only. “Small” is not a guarantee against restrictions, and a message being transactional does not automatically exempt the number or the sending method from WhatsApp’s rules.
What linked-device setup does and does not mean

Chat Automation’s listed connection method uses WhatsApp’s linked-device route. Its appeal is the straightforward setup and inexpensive entry point. Its suitability depends on more than order count: the number’s use, the audience, sending behavior and the consequences of an interruption all matter.

Do not decide solely by whether onboarding shows a QR code. A QR step can also appear in other WhatsApp onboarding arrangements. The important distinction is the actual integration behind it: a linked-device session versus the official business messaging platform. Ask which app is being installed and which connection method it will use.

If a small shop occasionally needs to reconnect and can handle a manual fallback, the older app may still be a practical fit. If an interruption would leave a warehouse without confirmation decisions or customers without important updates, I would choose Business API from the outset.
Why we built WhatFlow WhatsApp Business API

The newer product uses the official Meta Cloud API. It is our recommended route for stores that want a stronger operational foundation for automated business messaging. It replaces dependence on the older linked-device connection model with the official platform integration.

The Shopify experience matters just as much as the transport. WhatFlow Business API ties messaging to store events, template mapping, extensions and Shopify Flow, so an operator can work with the order behind the conversation. The team inbox helps colleagues answer the buyer after an automated update instead of leaving replies as a separate problem.

The official route still has rules. Business account eligibility, template requirements, customer permissions, message quality and WhatsApp enforcement remain relevant. Official API access does not make a number immune to restrictions or provide a promise that every message will arrive. Our recommendation is based on choosing the appropriate integration, not promising an exception to Meta’s policies.
Pricing: compare the two app bills separately

The older Chat Automation listing offers a free plan with 50 included sends and a $0.01 rate above that allowance. Its Starter is $4.99 with 1,000 included sends; Growth is $9.99 with 2,000; Professional is $14.99 with 4,000; Enterprise is $24.99 with 7,500. Those listed tiers show $0.01 above their allowances. An Ultimate subscription is listed at $49.99; confirm its current usage terms before budgeting beyond the explicitly displayed allowances.

Business API has different allowances. Its Free plan includes 100 sends, then $0.01 each. Starter is $4.99 with 2,000 sends, then $0.005; Plus is $9.99 with 5,000, then $0.004. Growth is $29 with 20,000, Scale is $49.99 with 40,000 and Ultimate is $99 with 75,000, with their respective overage rates shown on the official listing.

These are app-side prices in US dollars, billed on the listing’s 30-day cycle. Business API also needs the applicable Meta delivery charges, which depend on destination, message category and eligibility. The older linked-device app does not use the same Cloud API template-fee model. That difference can make its total sending cost attractive for modest transactional workloads, but the lower bill needs to be weighed against connection suitability.
A 5,000-message example, without hiding Meta fees

At 5,000 sends in one billing cycle, Business API Plus has a $9.99 app-side bill before applicable Meta fees and tax. In the older app, the displayed Professional allowance plus 1,000 overage sends costs $24.99; Enterprise also costs $24.99 and includes 7,500 sends. This illustrates why “the linked-device app always has the lower software bill” would be inaccurate.

The difference is $15 before Meta fees. If the Business API workload incurred $15 of Meta charges, its combined app-and-Meta amount would be $24.99 in this example. That is a break-even illustration, not a quoted Meta rate: actual country, category and eligible free-message treatment determine the real amount. Compare the full bill rather than either app’s subscription alone.

For transactional work, classification matters. A genuine order update is a different use case from a promotional offer attached to an order message. Check Meta’s current definitions and rates rather than assuming that calling a message transactional makes it free.
What Business API includes as the team grows

All WhatFlow Business API plans provide the same feature access, including Free. They differ by messaging allowances and rates. We do not make the merchant buy a higher feature edition merely to access another part of the product.

The Business API team inbox has no seat fees. A founder, support colleague and fulfillment operator can participate without adding a per-person subscription. Theme-matched WhatsApp buttons are free forever. Free feature access and a free storefront button are separate from the cost of automated sending and applicable Meta delivery fees.
Those are Business API policies. When comparing the older app, use its own current listing and configuration rather than transferring every price or entitlement from one product to the other.
How I would choose for a real Shopify store

A startup with a handful of daily orders, a tight budget and a workable manual fallback can consider Chat Automation after reviewing the linked-device tradeoffs. I would keep its purpose narrow and useful, rather than treating its low entry cost as a reason to maximize sending volume.

A store with a growing team, time-sensitive order processes or a serious campaign program should start with Business API. The official platform route, Shopify integration, included inbox and all-features model are a more appropriate foundation for the work that follows as the business grows.

Before switching an existing number, confirm its eligibility, any supported migration or coexistence arrangement and which history or settings can be retained. Test one complete journey and the human reply before cutting over. Moving to the newer app should be a planned change, not a rushed reaction to a single bad connection.
Our track record and our 2027 ambition

The newer app is a newer product, not a new team with no Shopify history. The two listings show the same developer and a merchant-facing history beginning in 2024. We want the newer Business API product to earn trust through the experience it delivers today, while learning from what merchants told us about the older integration.

My ambition is to make WhatFlow a leading choice for Shopify WhatsApp by the end of 2027. That is a goal we have to earn, not a verified forecast, a guaranteed number-one position or evidence that we are growing faster than every other app. For the merchant choosing today, the useful evidence is the correct listing, the working integration, transparent pricing and a team that explains the tradeoffs clearly.

faqs.answer: The 3.9-star rating belongs to the older WhatFlow: Whatsapp Automation app, launched October 21, 2024. faqs.question: Are WhatFlow Chat Automation and WhatFlow Business API the same app?
faqs.answer: No. They are separate Shopify apps from Scrptble. Chat Automation refers to the older WhatFlow: Whatsapp Automation listing at apps.shopify.com/whatflow. Business API is the newer official Meta Cloud API product at apps.shopify.com/whatflow-official-api. Their connection methods, pricing allowances, launch dates and review histories differ.

faqs.question: Which WhatFlow app is recommended for small or startup stores?
faqs.answer: The founder currently recommends considering linked-device Chat Automation only for small and startup stores with modest workloads and tolerance for connection interruptions. Small stores can also choose Business API, especially when their order communication is important to operations.

faqs.question: Which WhatFlow app is recommended for growing Shopify stores?
faqs.answer: WhatFlow WhatsApp Business API is the founder’s recommendation for growing stores and important automated messaging. It uses the official Meta Cloud API and includes Shopify-connected workflows and a team inbox without seat fees.

faqs.question: Did stricter WhatsApp enforcement cause every negative WhatFlow review?
faqs.answer: That has not been established. WhatFlow’s founder reports that changes in enforcement and linked-device connection behavior affected some merchants, especially at larger workloads. Public reviews also describe connection problems. This provides context, but it does not establish one cause for every negative review or dismiss merchants’ experiences.

faqs.question: Is WhatFlow Business API ban-proof?
faqs.answer: No. Using the official Meta Cloud API does not exempt a business from WhatsApp policies, eligibility requirements, template rules or quality enforcement. It is the official integration route WhatFlow recommends for production business messaging, not a guarantee against restrictions.

faqs.question: Is Chat Automation always cheaper than Business API?
faqs.answer: No. Its linked-device model can have attractive total costs for modest workloads, but the app allowances differ. At 5,000 sends, the displayed Business API Plus app fee is $9.99 before applicable Meta fees, while the older app’s Professional-with-overage or Enterprise amount is $24.99 before tax. Compare the combined bill and operational suitability.

faqs.question: Does Business API charge per inbox seat or restrict features on Free?
faqs.answer: No. WhatFlow Business API offers all features on every plan, has no team-inbox seat fees and provides free-forever theme-matched WhatsApp buttons. Messaging allowances and rates differ, and applicable Meta delivery fees remain separate.

faqs.question: Has WhatFlow been available on Shopify for more than two years?
faqs.answer: The older WhatFlow: Whatsapp Automation listing launched on October 21, 2024, which is more than two years before this guide’s October 24, 2026 review date. The separate Business API listing launched on May 8, 2026.

faqs.question: Will WhatFlow be the number-one Shopify WhatsApp app in 2027?
faqs.answer: That is not an established forecast. Safwan Adnan’s stated ambition is for WhatFlow to become a leading Shopify WhatsApp choice by the end of 2027. Future rankings and relative growth have not been verified or guaranteed.

children.text: The decision behind this comparison

SleekFlow combines an omnichannel inbox, automated flows and conversational commerce tools. Its pricing materials also describe CRM, analytics and service capabilities. That breadth is useful to teams organizing customer communication across departments; it also calls for a more detailed scope than simply adding WhatsApp to Shopify.

I’m Safwan Adnan, co-founder and CEO of WhatFlow. My recommendation starts with the store’s actual work: the order that needs a message, the customer who replies and the colleague who has to help. A useful comparison should explain why our approach fits that work, while being honest about what the alternative does well.
Pricing: what belongs in the comparison

Confirm the regional price, included users, contacts and automation allowances for the selected package. Include WhatsApp delivery costs and any commerce or AI components required for the proposed workflow. Regional pricing should retain its original currency and billing period.
A realistic Shopify scenario

A retailer has online staff, a physical sales team and a centralized service desk. Test how ownership passes between those groups, and whether a Shopify operator can still investigate a failed order update without waiting for another department.
Why WhatFlow is a strong fit for store operations
WhatFlow is an appealing choice for the Shopify portion of that work because its inbox has no seat fees and its plans preserve full feature access at every volume.

An inbox is only one part of a customer journey. Someone still needs to know which order the customer means and what should happen next. For a Shopify merchant, that context is often more useful than adding another independent contact database. WhatFlow brings Shopify events, message templates and the human response into a focused operating workflow. Its native-feeling extensions matter because store staff already spend their day managing the underlying orders.
Feature access and the people who use the inbox

We built WhatFlow so the first plan does not feel like an intentionally incomplete product. Every feature is available whether the store chooses Free or the highest paid plan. The subscription choice changes messaging allowances and rates, not access to the inbox, Shopify integrations or other features. A merchant can start with one workflow and add another without purchasing a new feature edition.

The team inbox has no seat fees. If the founder, a support colleague and someone in fulfillment all need to participate, adding those people does not create a per-user WhatFlow subscription. That is particularly useful when store staff share responsibilities rather than operating a large formal support department.
A worked WhatFlow cost example

For a concrete baseline, consider 40,000 sent messages in a month. Among the listed WhatFlow plans, Scale produces an app-side cost of $49.99 at that volume. This calculation uses its $49.99 base, 40,000 included sends and $0.002 rate above the allowance. It assumes a single monthly allowance and does not include tax or Meta delivery charges. It is a planning example, not a combined quote for every possible message category or destination.

Keep three lines in the budget: the application, applicable WhatsApp delivery fees, and any separate implementation or services. Meta pricing varies by destination and category, and some service or qualifying utility messages have different treatment. An app allowance does not override Meta’s rules. The current installation terms and rate pages should be checked before committing a campaign budget.
What I would test before switching

Use the scenario above with controlled recipients and real test-order values. Have the person who will maintain the workflow edit a template and have another person handle a reply. Confirm the required plan, billing units and number migration or coexistence eligibility before moving a live channel. A polished demo is useful, but the handoff after the message is what the store will live with.
SleekFlow can be useful when the organization wants a broader conversation platform and will use its cross-department tooling.

For a Shopify merchant prioritizing affordable WhatsApp operations, I would start with WhatFlow: whatFlow is an appealing choice for the Shopify portion of that work because its inbox has no seat fees and its plans preserve full feature access at every volume.

children.text: The decision behind this comparison

HubSpot Service Hub connects service activity with CRM records and a wider marketing and sales ecosystem. Its value is often the shared customer record across departments, rather than the lowest possible cost of sending a Shopify notification.

I’m Safwan Adnan, co-founder and CEO of WhatFlow. My recommendation starts with the store’s actual work: the order that needs a message, the customer who replies and the colleague who has to help. A useful comparison should explain why our approach fits that work, while being honest about what the alternative does well.
Pricing: what belongs in the comparison

Ask for the exact Service Hub edition, seats, onboarding, WhatsApp availability and any other Hub subscriptions required. A broad CRM package can include capabilities unrelated to the store’s immediate WhatsApp job; include them only if the business will actually use them.
A realistic Shopify scenario

A sales team wants a contact timeline while store operations need an order confirmation recorded correctly. Agree which record owns the action and show the handoff when the same buyer has both an open deal and a Shopify order.
Why WhatFlow is a strong fit for store operations
WhatFlow offers Shopify-linked WhatsApp and a no-seat-fee inbox without requiring a larger CRM subscription. It can complement the customer record the business already maintains elsewhere.

Service-suite features can be valuable, but the buying question should begin with the cases the store actually handles. A short order question, a delivery exception and a multi-day dispute may need different processes. WhatFlow is attractive for the Shopify WhatsApp layer because staff can participate without a seat charge and use the complete feature set. Keep any existing service system that still solves a separate, important job.
Feature access and the people who use the inbox

The team inbox has no seat fees. If the founder, a support colleague and someone in fulfillment all need to participate, adding those people does not create a per-user WhatFlow subscription. That is particularly useful when store staff share responsibilities rather than operating a large formal support department.

The storefront WhatsApp buttons remain free forever and can fit the Shopify theme and design. The button is an entry point, not a promise of unlimited free automated sends. Automated messaging still follows the selected allowance and applicable delivery rules. Keeping those two costs separate makes the free offering easier to understand.
A worked WhatFlow cost example

For a concrete baseline, consider 40,000 sent messages in a month. Among the listed WhatFlow plans, Scale produces an app-side cost of $49.99 at that volume. This calculation uses its $49.99 base, 40,000 included sends and $0.002 rate above the allowance. It assumes a single monthly allowance and does not include tax or Meta delivery charges. It is a planning example, not a combined quote for every possible message category or destination.

Keep three lines in the budget: the application, applicable WhatsApp delivery fees, and any separate implementation or services. Meta pricing varies by destination and category, and some service or qualifying utility messages have different treatment. An app allowance does not override Meta’s rules. The current installation terms and rate pages should be checked before committing a campaign budget.
What I would test before switching

Use the scenario above with controlled recipients and real test-order values. Have the person who will maintain the workflow edit a template and have another person handle a reply. Confirm the required plan, billing units and number migration or coexistence eligibility before moving a live channel. A polished demo is useful, but the handoff after the message is what the store will live with.
HubSpot can be appropriate when unifying marketing, sales and service records is the project and the business has budgeted for that scope.

For a Shopify merchant prioritizing affordable WhatsApp operations, I would start with WhatFlow: whatFlow offers Shopify-linked WhatsApp and a no-seat-fee inbox without requiring a larger CRM subscription. It can complement the customer record the business already maintains elsewhere.

children.text: The decision behind this comparison

Chatfuel provides AI and conversational automation for WhatsApp and social channels. Its appeal is automating customer acquisition and responses, while a Shopify merchant also needs dependable order context and an operating process for exceptions.

I’m Safwan Adnan, co-founder and CEO of WhatFlow. My recommendation starts with the store’s actual work: the order that needs a message, the customer who replies and the colleague who has to help. A useful comparison should explain why our approach fits that work, while being honest about what the alternative does well.
Pricing: what belongs in the comparison

Chatfuel’s pricing page displays Business at $18 per month billed yearly, or $216 for the year, with an AI-credit allowance. Confirm the current offer, channel usage and Meta wallet charges. A credit is not automatically equivalent to one sent order notification.
A realistic Shopify scenario
A store wants an automated answer to a product question, followed by a human handling a changed delivery address. Examine the boundary between the bot and the person who must act on the order.
Why WhatFlow is a strong fit for store operations

WhatFlow prioritizes the Shopify operational workflow and includes the inbox without seat fees or plan-based feature gates. That is useful when the merchant wants predictable access rather than a separate bot project.

An inbox is only one part of a customer journey. Someone still needs to know which order the customer means and what should happen next. For a Shopify merchant, that context is often more useful than adding another independent contact database. WhatFlow brings Shopify events, message templates and the human response into a focused operating workflow. Its native-feeling extensions matter because store staff already spend their day managing the underlying orders.
Feature access and the people who use the inbox

The team inbox has no seat fees. If the founder, a support colleague and someone in fulfillment all need to participate, adding those people does not create a per-user WhatFlow subscription. That is particularly useful when store staff share responsibilities rather than operating a large formal support department.

The storefront WhatsApp buttons remain free forever and can fit the Shopify theme and design. The button is an entry point, not a promise of unlimited free automated sends. Automated messaging still follows the selected allowance and applicable delivery rules. Keeping those two costs separate makes the free offering easier to understand.
A worked WhatFlow cost example

For a concrete baseline, consider 1,000 sent messages in a month. Among the listed WhatFlow plans, Starter produces an app-side cost of $4.99 at that volume. This calculation uses its $4.99 base, 2,000 included sends and $0.005 rate above the allowance. It assumes a single monthly allowance and does not include tax or Meta delivery charges. It is a planning example, not a combined quote for every possible message category or destination.

Keep three lines in the budget: the application, applicable WhatsApp delivery fees, and any separate implementation or services. Meta pricing varies by destination and category, and some service or qualifying utility messages have different treatment. An app allowance does not override Meta’s rules. The current installation terms and rate pages should be checked before committing a campaign budget.
What I would test before switching

Use the scenario above with controlled recipients and real test-order values. Have the person who will maintain the workflow edit a template and have another person handle a reply. Confirm the required plan, billing units and number migration or coexistence eligibility before moving a live channel. A polished demo is useful, but the handoff after the message is what the store will live with.
Chatfuel may be preferable when automated social or AI conversations are the main purchase.

For a Shopify merchant prioritizing affordable WhatsApp operations, I would start with WhatFlow: whatFlow prioritizes the Shopify operational workflow and includes the inbox without seat fees or plan-based feature gates. That is useful when the merchant wants predictable access rather than a separate bot project.

I’m Safwan Adnan, co-founder and CEO of WhatFlow. My recommendation starts with the store’s actual work: the order that needs a message, the customer who replies and the colleague who has to help. A useful comparison should explain why our approach fits that work, while being honest about what the alternative does well.
Pricing: what belongs in the comparison

Use a current proposal covering the required channels, customer data, implementation and usage. A quote for enterprise engagement should be judged on the outcomes the business will actually use; it is not a public price for a simple WhatsApp order workflow.
A realistic Shopify scenario

A data team wants to orchestrate mobile, web and store journeys from a common audience. Identify which part of that architecture must live centrally and which order-related actions can remain close to Shopify.
Why WhatFlow is a strong fit for store operations

WhatFlow is an accessible way to run the Shopify WhatsApp layer with published plans, no seat fees and full feature access. It can help a store start useful workflows before a larger engagement project is complete.

An inbox is only one part of a customer journey. Someone still needs to know which order the customer means and what should happen next. For a Shopify merchant, that context is often more useful than adding another independent contact database. WhatFlow brings Shopify events, message templates and the human response into a focused operating workflow. Its native-feeling extensions matter because store staff already spend their day managing the underlying orders.
Feature access and the people who use the inbox

The storefront WhatsApp buttons remain free forever and can fit the Shopify theme and design. The button is an entry point, not a promise of unlimited free automated sends. Automated messaging still follows the selected allowance and applicable delivery rules. Keeping those two costs separate makes the free offering easier to understand.

We built WhatFlow so the first plan does not feel like an intentionally incomplete product. Every feature is available whether the store chooses Free or the highest paid plan. The subscription choice changes messaging allowances and rates, not access to the inbox, Shopify integrations or other features. A merchant can start with one workflow and add another without purchasing a new feature edition.

It is a planning example, not a combined quote for every possible message category or destination.

The current installation terms and rate pages should be checked before committing a campaign budget.

A polished demo is useful, but the handoff after the message is what the store will live with.

children.text: The decision behind this comparison

Dondy is a Shopify WhatsApp competitor with a Built for Shopify badge, ecommerce automation, AI-related tools, integrations and a free button offering. Its Shopify integration is a real strength. The strongest WhatFlow comparison is therefore the commercial model and access to the functions the merchant needs.

I’m Safwan Adnan, co-founder and CEO of WhatFlow. My recommendation starts with the store’s actual work: the order that needs a message, the customer who replies and the colleague who has to help. A useful comparison should explain why our approach fits that work, while being honest about what the alternative does well.
Pricing: what belongs in the comparison

Dondy’s listing displays Free, Pro at $6.99 per month, Power Automation at $79.99 and Elite at $159.99. Its paid packages and message rates have different inclusions; verify the current details before calculating a total. WhatFlow Starter at $4.99 and Plus at $9.99 provide full feature access, with 2,000 and 5,000 sends respectively before overage and applicable Meta fees.
A realistic Shopify scenario

A merchant begins with a free button, then wants automated messages and a usable team inbox. Compare the exact package needed for that second stage instead of assuming the free widget represents the whole automation product.
Why WhatFlow is a strong fit for store operations
WhatFlow’s all-features policy means the store chooses a plan for message volume rather than moving to a larger edition to access another feature. No seat fees apply to its team inbox.

The useful integration test starts after the message arrives. Open the Shopify order, check its current state and ask a second colleague to continue the conversation. An app can advertise Shopify connectivity while still making routine work awkward. WhatFlow’s extensions, store-event templates and Flow support are intended to keep that work close to the store. The demo screenshot shows a working configuration surface rather than a sales mockup.
Feature access and the people who use the inbox

We built WhatFlow so the first plan does not feel like an intentionally incomplete product. Every feature is available whether the store chooses Free or the highest paid plan. The subscription choice changes messaging allowances and rates, not access to the inbox, Shopify integrations or other features. A merchant can start with one workflow and add another without purchasing a new feature edition.

The team inbox has no seat fees. If the founder, a support colleague and someone in fulfillment all need to participate, adding those people does not create a per-user WhatFlow subscription. That is particularly useful when store staff share responsibilities rather than operating a large formal support department.
A worked WhatFlow cost example

For a concrete baseline, consider 20,000 sent messages in a month. Among the listed WhatFlow plans, Growth produces an app-side cost of $29.00 at that volume. This calculation uses its $29.00 base, 20,000 included sends and $0.0025 rate above the allowance. It assumes a single monthly allowance and does not include tax or Meta delivery charges. It is a planning example, not a combined quote for every possible message category or destination.

Keep three lines in the budget: the application, applicable WhatsApp delivery fees, and any separate implementation or services. Meta pricing varies by destination and category, and some service or qualifying utility messages have different treatment. An app allowance does not override Meta’s rules. The current installation terms and rate pages should be checked before committing a campaign budget.
Dondy’s acquisition: what is confirmed and what to ask

Dondy announced that it joined Circeus and became part of Shop Circle in July 2026. Its announcement says the product, team, support and customer accounts would continue. The buyer has also described a broader AI-led and upmarket strategy. That is a published direction, rather than evidence that the company has no direction.

For a Shopify merchant, the useful question is how that roadmap fits the store. Ask for the current plan’s pricing, included users, support terms and the capabilities you will need next. Future commercial changes remain unknown; the acquisition alone does not establish that prices will rise or service will worsen.

If your priority is affordable Shopify WhatsApp with all features available and no inbox seat fees, WhatFlow Business API offers a clear current proposition without requiring you to buy into a broader enterprise AI program. Compare that present-day fit with the actual Dondy proposal.
Which WhatFlow app is this Dondy comparison about?

This guide compares Dondy with WhatFlow WhatsApp Business API, our official Meta Cloud API app. It is separate from the older linked-device WhatFlow Chat Automation app. On October 24, 2026, Shopify showed 5.0 stars for Business API and 3.9 for the older app. Those ratings should not be combined or transferred between listings. Our detailed Chat Automation versus Business API guide explains the connection methods, intended store sizes and review context.
What I would test before switching

Use the scenario above with controlled recipients and real test-order values. Have the person who will maintain the workflow edit a template and have another person handle a reply. Confirm the required plan, billing units and number migration or coexistence eligibility before moving a live channel. A polished demo is useful, but the handoff after the message is what the store will live with.
Dondy is worth evaluating for its particular AI, integrations and Shopify experience. WhatFlow’s case is strong without pretending that Dondy lacks Shopify integration or a free option.

That is where WhatsApp becomes particularly attractive for a Shopify store whose customers already use it. The customer can move from an update to a question without starting again in a different support channel.

SMS has a valuable reach advantage: the recipient does not need WhatsApp installed or a mobile data connection to receive an ordinary text. Send the same useful order update to permissioned test recipients through each channel. Check how the product context, tracking link and reply appear. Record delivery, actual billed units and whether the team can answer the resulting question against the correct order.

Write down the intended audience, trigger, message and owner before enabling the workflow. Use test recipients first and include an awkward case, not only the ideal purchase. Start with the scenario in this guide and define what success means for it: a usable reply, a correctly handled order or a genuinely helpful customer interaction. Keep existing channels that still serve their purpose. Coordinate timing so the same buyer does not receive overlapping messages simply because several tools are available.

I’m Safwan Adnan, co-founder and CEO of WhatFlow. We put particular emphasis on Shopify integration because a message is rarely the entire job. A controlled test before launch

Ask a test shopper a product question, then have them leave the website and return with an order question later. Check how much context survives and how easily a second teammate can continue the response.

children.text: Start with the customer’s job

A review request works best when the customer has had a fair chance to use the product. WhatsApp can make the request feel like a natural follow-up, especially if the same conversation already contains useful order updates.
Where each approach helps

Email remains useful for richer product context and established review programs. Neither channel should pressure the customer, imply that only positive reviews are welcome or send a request before the experience is complete.
The practical cost difference

Count review requests separately from order messages and include the applicable template category and delivery fee. A request that repeats across several channels can increase cost and irritation without producing more useful feedback.
Why I would use WhatFlow for this workflow
WhatFlow supports Shopify-focused follow-up and relevant integration workflows, with feature access available on every plan rather than reserved for a larger subscription.

I’m Safwan Adnan, co-founder and CEO of WhatFlow. We put particular emphasis on Shopify integration because a message is rarely the entire job. Someone needs to understand the store event behind it, answer the buyer and take the next useful action. The extensions and Shopify-connected configuration are intended to make that feel like part of running the store rather than managing an unrelated communications project.
A controlled test before launch
Test the timing, product link and review destination with a completed test purchase. Coordinate with the existing review platform so one delivery does not trigger several overlapping requests.

Write down the intended audience, trigger, message and owner before enabling the workflow. Use test recipients first and include an awkward case, not only the ideal purchase. When the buyer replies, ask another teammate to continue the conversation. The result should be understandable without relying on the first person’s memory. This is a suggested evaluation method, not a claim that we measured a particular uplift in another store.
WhatFlow’s allowance and team costs

For a concrete baseline, consider 1,000 sent messages in a month. Among the listed WhatFlow plans, Starter produces an app-side cost of $4.99 at that volume. This calculation uses its $4.99 base, 2,000 included sends and $0.005 rate above the allowance. It assumes a single monthly allowance and does not include tax or Meta delivery charges. It is a planning example, not a combined quote for every possible message category or destination.

Keep three lines in the budget: the application, applicable WhatsApp delivery fees, and any separate implementation or services. Meta pricing varies by destination and category, and some service or qualifying utility messages have different treatment. An app allowance does not override Meta’s rules. The current installation terms and rate pages should be checked before committing a campaign budget.
The features you keep as the store grows

The storefront WhatsApp buttons remain free forever and can fit the Shopify theme and design. The button is an entry point, not a promise of unlimited free automated sends. Automated messaging still follows the selected allowance and applicable delivery rules. Keeping those two costs separate makes the free offering easier to understand.

We built WhatFlow so the first plan does not feel like an intentionally incomplete product. Every feature is available whether the store chooses Free or the highest paid plan. The subscription choice changes messaging allowances and rates, not access to the inbox, Shopify integrations or other features. A merchant can start with one workflow and add another without purchasing a new feature edition.
A sensible first rollout

Start with the scenario in this guide and define what success means for it: a usable reply, a correctly handled order or a genuinely helpful customer interaction. Keep existing channels that still serve their purpose. Coordinate timing so the same buyer does not receive overlapping messages simply because several tools are available.

As the store grows, the next workflow should not require buying access to another feature tier. WhatFlow keeps feature access consistent and lets the plan decision follow messaging needs.

Its catalog and everyday messaging tools are useful, and eligible businesses may also see newer AI features. I’m Safwan Adnan, co-founder and CEO of WhatFlow. My recommendation starts with the store’s actual work: the order that needs a message, the customer who replies and the colleague who has to help. A useful comparison should explain why our approach fits that work, while being honest about what the alternative does well.
Pricing: what belongs in the comparison

The app’s free entry point is a real advantage. The comparison is the work surrounding a message: finding the order, selecting the correct details, handling repeated updates and coordinating staff. WhatFlow also has a free plan and a free-forever storefront button, while automated sends follow the selected allowance and delivery rules.
A realistic Shopify scenario

A founder copies order details into individual chats every evening. That can work at first, but a missed fulfillment update or an unanswered reply exposes the limits of a process that depends entirely on someone remembering the next step.
What WhatFlow adds to evaluate

In the WhatFlow demo Shopify app, event automations and template mappings give the store a defined process for order confirmations, fulfillment messages and checkout reminders. The operator can inspect the fields and preview instead of manually composing each update.

The benefit to test is whether the process reduces repetitive work while preserving useful customer communication. A message sent automatically still needs accurate data, sensible timing and someone ready to answer.
Why WhatFlow is a strong fit for store operations

WhatFlow adds Shopify-triggered messages, mapped store data and an included team inbox without per-seat fees. It turns repeatable store events into a maintained workflow while keeping humans available for the exceptions.

An inbox is only one part of a customer journey. Someone still needs to know which order the customer means and what should happen next. For a Shopify merchant, that context is often more useful than adding another independent contact database. WhatFlow brings Shopify events, message templates and the human response into a focused operating workflow. Its native-feeling extensions matter because store staff already spend their day managing the underlying orders.

The storefront WhatsApp buttons remain free forever and can fit the Shopify theme and design. The button is an entry point, not a promise of unlimited free automated sends. Automated messaging still follows the selected allowance and applicable delivery rules. Keeping those two costs separate makes the free offering easier to understand.

The subscription choice changes messaging allowances and rates, not access to the inbox, Shopify integrations or other features. A merchant can start with one workflow and add another without purchasing a new feature edition.

Meta pricing varies by destination and category, and some service or qualifying utility messages have different treatment. An app allowance does not override Meta’s rules. The current installation terms and rate pages should be checked before committing a campaign budget.
What I would test before switching

Use the scenario above with controlled recipients and real test-order values. Have the person who will maintain the workflow edit a template and have another person handle a reply. Confirm the required plan, billing units and number migration or coexistence eligibility before moving a live channel. A polished demo is useful, but the handoff after the message is what the store will live with.

Gallabox's website presents a customer journey spanning inquiry capture, qualification, nurturing, conversion and retention. children.text: The decision behind this comparison

respond.io is a conversation platform spanning channels, automation and customer-facing teams. Its pricing combines plan scope, included users and monthly active contacts. Those units reflect a broader operating model than simply counting a Shopify store’s outbound messages.

I’m Safwan Adnan, co-founder and CEO of WhatFlow. My recommendation starts with the store’s actual work: the order that needs a message, the customer who replies and the colleague who has to help. A useful comparison should explain why our approach fits that work, while being honest about what the alternative does well.
Pricing: what belongs in the comparison

The pricing page lists included-user allowances of five or ten depending on plan, with additional-user charges displayed at $12, $20 or $24 per month for the relevant tiers. Confirm the active-contact allowance and WhatsApp charges too. Avoid comparing only the price of an extra user with the cost of an entire application.
A realistic Shopify scenario

A sales organization wants lead routing across several channels, while the store team mainly needs shipping and cart conversations. Identify which responsibility is driving the purchase before paying for the larger operating model.
Where respond.io focuses

Respond.io describes a platform that brings customer touchpoints, CRMs and AI agents into a team inbox. Its site presents lead capture, qualification, routing, bookings and ongoing conversations across channels. That makes it relevant when sales and support staff need to manage a continuing customer relationship.
Confirm the specific channels, integrations and account allowances in the proposed plan. A broad conversation platform can support many designs, but your store still needs a defined implementation.
Where WhatFlow starts

The WhatFlow demo app organizes automations around Shopify events. The template editor maps fields such as customer name, order total and checkout link into an outgoing message. This gives a store operator a concrete place to maintain an order update or a recovery reminder.

That approach should be judged on its event coverage and clarity, rather than on whether it resembles a full sales CRM. Equally, a conversation platform should be judged on the lead workflow your team actually needs.
Why WhatFlow is a strong fit for store operations
WhatFlow has no seat fees and does not gate its Shopify features by plan. A store can invite the people who actually handle orders without turning each handoff into another recurring user charge.

An inbox is only one part of a customer journey. Someone still needs to know which order the customer means and what should happen next. For a Shopify merchant, that context is often more useful than adding another independent contact database. WhatFlow brings Shopify events, message templates and the human response into a focused operating workflow. Its native-feeling extensions matter because store staff already spend their day managing the underlying orders.
Feature access and the people who use the inbox

The storefront WhatsApp buttons remain free forever and can fit the Shopify theme and design. The button is an entry point, not a promise of unlimited free automated sends. Automated messaging still follows the selected allowance and applicable delivery rules. Keeping those two costs separate makes the free offering easier to understand.

We built WhatFlow so the first plan does not feel like an intentionally incomplete product. Every feature is available whether the store chooses Free or the highest paid plan. The subscription choice changes messaging allowances and rates, not access to the inbox, Shopify integrations or other features. A merchant can start with one workflow and add another without purchasing a new feature edition.
A worked WhatFlow cost example

For a concrete baseline, consider 40,000 sent messages in a month. Among the listed WhatFlow plans, Scale produces an app-side cost of $49.99 at that volume. This calculation uses its $49.99 base, 40,000 included sends and $0.002 rate above the allowance. It assumes a single monthly allowance and does not include tax or Meta delivery charges. It is a planning example, not a combined quote for every possible message category or destination.

Keep three lines in the budget: the application, applicable WhatsApp delivery fees, and any separate implementation or services. Meta pricing varies by destination and category, and some service or qualifying utility messages have different treatment. An app allowance does not override Meta’s rules. The current installation terms and rate pages should be checked before committing a campaign budget.
What I would test before switching

Use the scenario above with controlled recipients and real test-order values. Have the person who will maintain the workflow edit a template and have another person handle a reply. Confirm the required plan, billing units and number migration or coexistence eligibility before moving a live channel. A polished demo is useful, but the handoff after the message is what the store will live with.

children.text: The decision behind this comparison

Klaviyo now offers WhatsApp as part of its customer engagement ecosystem. Comparing WhatFlow with an outdated description of Klaviyo as email-only would be misleading. Its case is unified customer data and coordinated marketing across channels.

I’m Safwan Adnan, co-founder and CEO of WhatFlow. My recommendation starts with the store’s actual work: the order that needs a message, the customer who replies and the colleague who has to help. A useful comparison should explain why our approach fits that work, while being honest about what the alternative does well.
Pricing: what belongs in the comparison

Klaviyo pricing depends on the selected products, audience and usage. Obtain a quote that includes WhatsApp for the relevant countries and message categories. Do not use a free email allowance as though it were a free WhatsApp package, or assume an email subscription automatically includes the desired WhatsApp sends.
A realistic Shopify scenario

A shopper receives an email campaign and a WhatsApp checkout reminder before buying. Agree which system owns suppression, audience updates and attribution, so the same order does not become two separate revenue claims.
What Klaviyo advertises today

Klaviyo's WhatsApp page describes marketing and utility messages, customer-data-driven segments, cart reminders and order or shipping updates. It also presents service conversations and connections between marketing and customer support. Confirm availability, plan terms and market-specific restrictions for your account during evaluation.

Those features make Klaviyo relevant when the team already depends on its profiles and marketing workflows. They do not automatically establish that every Shopify operational requirement is covered in the way your fulfillment team expects.
Where WhatFlow fits

The WhatFlow demo app starts with Shopify events and mapped message templates. Order confirmation, fulfillment and abandoned checkout are explicit automation types. That offers a concrete evaluation path for a store whose primary goal is to make those customer updates run consistently.
A store does not have to replace its email platform to test that approach. The important work is defining which system owns which messages and how overlapping follow-ups will be avoided.
Why WhatFlow is a strong fit for store operations

WhatFlow offers a practical way to add WhatsApp operations without replacing the store’s existing email platform. The free-forever storefront button, no-seat-fee inbox and all-features plans help keep that addition affordable.

The useful integration test starts after the message arrives. Open the Shopify order, check its current state and ask a second colleague to continue the conversation. An app can advertise Shopify connectivity while still making routine work awkward. WhatFlow’s extensions, store-event templates and Flow support are intended to keep that work close to the store. The demo screenshot shows a working configuration surface rather than a sales mockup.
Feature access and the people who use the inbox

The team inbox has no seat fees. If the founder, a support colleague and someone in fulfillment all need to participate, adding those people does not create a per-user WhatFlow subscription. That is particularly useful when store staff share responsibilities rather than operating a large formal support department.

The storefront WhatsApp buttons remain free forever and can fit the Shopify theme and design. The button is an entry point, not a promise of unlimited free automated sends. Automated messaging still follows the selected allowance and applicable delivery rules. Keeping those two costs separate makes the free offering easier to understand.
A worked WhatFlow cost example

For a concrete baseline, consider 10,000 sent messages in a month. Among the listed WhatFlow plans, Growth produces an app-side cost of $29.00 at that volume. This calculation uses its $29.00 base, 20,000 included sends and $0.0025 rate above the allowance. It assumes a single monthly allowance and does not include tax or Meta delivery charges. It is a planning example, not a combined quote for every possible message category or destination.

Keep three lines in the budget: the application, applicable WhatsApp delivery fees, and any separate implementation or services. Meta pricing varies by destination and category, and some service or qualifying utility messages have different treatment. An app allowance does not override Meta’s rules. The current installation terms and rate pages should be checked before committing a campaign budget.
What I would test before switching

Use the scenario above with controlled recipients and real test-order values. Have the person who will maintain the workflow edit a template and have another person handle a reply. Confirm the required plan, billing units and number migration or coexistence eligibility before moving a live channel. A polished demo is useful, but the handoff after the message is what the store will live with.
Klaviyo can be a strong fit when a dedicated lifecycle team needs its unified data and cross-channel orchestration rather than a focused Shopify WhatsApp app.

children.text: The decision behind this comparison

QuickReply.ai documents Shopify journeys and ecommerce automations. It should be evaluated as an ecommerce messaging product, not dismissed as a generic chatbot. The useful distinction is how its journey tooling, commercial terms and everyday operating process compare with WhatFlow’s Shopify-first approach.

I’m Safwan Adnan, co-founder and CEO of WhatFlow. My recommendation starts with the store’s actual work: the order that needs a message, the customer who replies and the colleague who has to help. A useful comparison should explain why our approach fits that work, while being honest about what the alternative does well.
Pricing: what belongs in the comparison

Confirm the current plan and messaging terms directly with QuickReply.ai. Ask whether the quoted package includes the journeys, support access, users and reporting shown in the demo. An attractive headline becomes less useful if the workflow you actually want belongs to another package.
A realistic Shopify scenario

Build a cart reminder with a delay, then complete checkout before the delay expires. Review how the selected journey handles that completed order and whether an operator can investigate it without developer assistance.
What QuickReply.ai documents

QuickReply.ai's documentation describes a WhatsApp marketing automation platform with Shopify integration and two-way customer conversations. Its journey documentation explains triggers, wait steps, filters and exit conditions. Those are useful capabilities to explore when the goal involves several steps rather than one notification.
Ask for a demonstration using your required event and data fields. A journey that looks simple on a diagram can still depend on plan access, a third-party event or a particular integration.
Where WhatFlow makes the work visible

The WhatFlow demo template editor shows a trigger selector and explicit mappings for customer, order and checkout values. The abandoned checkout example includes a recovery URL button. That gives an operator a clear place to inspect what the customer should see.

There is also an important distinction between configuring a template and enabling an automation. In the demo store, automation cards show whether a template is selected. Your trial should verify both configuration and activation instead of assuming that an approved message is already running.
Why WhatFlow is a strong fit for store operations

WhatFlow’s all-features policy removes the need to choose a subscription based on access to one particular automation. The store can select its message allowance and keep the same inbox and Shopify feature access.

The useful integration test starts after the message arrives. Open the Shopify order, check its current state and ask a second colleague to continue the conversation. An app can advertise Shopify connectivity while still making routine work awkward. WhatFlow’s extensions, store-event templates and Flow support are intended to keep that work close to the store. The demo screenshot shows a working configuration surface rather than a sales mockup.
Feature access and the people who use the inbox

We built WhatFlow so the first plan does not feel like an intentionally incomplete product. Every feature is available whether the store chooses Free or the highest paid plan. The subscription choice changes messaging allowances and rates, not access to the inbox, Shopify integrations or other features. A merchant can start with one workflow and add another without purchasing a new feature edition.

The team inbox has no seat fees. If the founder, a support colleague and someone in fulfillment all need to participate, adding those people does not create a per-user WhatFlow subscription. That is particularly useful when store staff share responsibilities rather than operating a large formal support department.
A worked WhatFlow cost example

For a concrete baseline, consider 20,000 sent messages in a month. Among the listed WhatFlow plans, Growth produces an app-side cost of $29.00 at that volume. This calculation uses its $29.00 base, 20,000 included sends and $0.0025 rate above the allowance. It assumes a single monthly allowance and does not include tax or Meta delivery charges. It is a planning example, not a combined quote for every possible message category or destination.

Keep three lines in the budget: the application, applicable WhatsApp delivery fees, and any separate implementation or services. Meta pricing varies by destination and category, and some service or qualifying utility messages have different treatment. An app allowance does not override Meta’s rules. The current installation terms and rate pages should be checked before committing a campaign budget.
What I would test before switching

Use the scenario above with controlled recipients and real test-order values. Have the person who will maintain the workflow edit a template and have another person handle a reply. Confirm the required plan, billing units and number migration or coexistence eligibility before moving a live channel. A polished demo is useful, but the handoff after the message is what the store will live with.
QuickReply.ai is worth considering for teams that prefer its journey-building approach and receive a package that fits their actual send mix.

For a Shopify merchant prioritizing affordable WhatsApp operations, I would start with WhatFlow: whatFlow’s all-features policy removes the need to choose a subscription based on access to one particular automation. The store can select its message allowance and keep the same inbox and Shopify feature access.

An inbox is only one part of a customer journey. Someone still needs to know which order the customer means and what should happen next. For a Shopify merchant, that context is often more useful than adding another independent contact database. WhatFlow brings Shopify events, message templates and the human response into a focused operating workflow. Its native-feeling extensions matter because store staff already spend their day managing the underlying orders.
Feature access and the people who use the inbox

We built WhatFlow so the first plan does not feel like an intentionally incomplete product. Every feature is available whether the store chooses Free or the highest paid plan. The subscription choice changes messaging allowances and rates, not access to the inbox, Shopify integrations or other features. A merchant can start with one workflow and add another without purchasing a new feature edition.

The team inbox has no seat fees. If the founder, a support colleague and someone in fulfillment all need to participate, adding those people does not create a per-user WhatFlow subscription. That is particularly useful when store staff share responsibilities rather than operating a large formal support department.
A worked WhatFlow cost example

For a concrete baseline, consider 1,000 sent messages in a month. Among the listed WhatFlow plans, Starter produces an app-side cost of $4.99 at that volume. This calculation uses its $4.99 base, 2,000 included sends and $0.005 rate above the allowance. It assumes a single monthly allowance and does not include tax or Meta delivery charges. It is a planning example, not a combined quote for every possible message category or destination.

Keep three lines in the budget: the application, applicable WhatsApp delivery fees, and any separate implementation or services. Meta pricing varies by destination and category, and some service or qualifying utility messages have different treatment. An app allowance does not override Meta’s rules. The current installation terms and rate pages should be checked before committing a campaign budget.
What I would test before switching

Use the scenario above with controlled recipients and real test-order values. Have the person who will maintain the workflow edit a template and have another person handle a reply. Confirm the required plan, billing units and number migration or coexistence eligibility before moving a live channel. A polished demo is useful, but the handoff after the message is what the store will live with.
Wati can suit a wider WhatsApp sales organization that values its broader platform and is comfortable with the quoted plan and connector terms.

For a Shopify merchant prioritizing affordable WhatsApp operations, I would start with WhatFlow: whatFlow keeps the inbox accessible without seat charges and makes every feature available on every plan. The plan decision is about sending volume, rather than whether order automation or another colleague deserves an upgrade.
